Department of Linguistic and Cultural Evolution
Department of Primate Behavior and Evolution

nodes.label: Population genetics
nodes.description: The mathematical theory of how allele and genotype frequencies change over time under mutation, selection, drift, migration, and mating patterns — the formal backbone for interpreting ancient and modern genomic variation.

nodes.label: Human evolution
nodes.description: The broad evolutionary framework describing the origin and diversification of Homo sapiens and related hominins, which archaeogenetics tests directly against ancient genomic evidence.

nodes.label: Demographic history
nodes.description: Reconstruction of past population sizes, splits, contractions, and expansions from patterns of genetic variation, used to infer the lived history behind a genome.

nodes.label: Selection
nodes.description: The theory of differential reproductive success driving allele frequency change, distinguished in genomic data from drift by characteristic signatures (e.g. reduced diversity, extended haplotypes) around a selected locus.

nodes.label: Admixture
nodes.description: The theory and statistical modeling of gene flow between previously separated populations (including between Homo sapiens and archaic hominins), leaving detectable mosaic ancestry patterns in descendant genomes.

nodes.label: Migration models
nodes.description: Formal models of how populations move and exchange migrants across space and time, used to fit genomic data to candidate routes and rates of human dispersal.

nodes.label: Ancient DNA
nodes.description: DNA recovered from archaeological and paleontological remains (bone, teeth, sediment), typically degraded and contaminated, requiring specialized extraction and authentication methods.

nodes.label: Genomes
nodes.description: Complete or partial genomic sequences — ancient and modern — that serve as the department's core empirical material.

nodes.label: Archaic admixture
nodes.description: The genomic legacy of interbreeding between anatomically modern humans and archaic hominins such as Neanderthals and Denisovans.

nodes.label: Pathogens
nodes.description: Ancient microbial and viral DNA recovered alongside or from host remains, used to track the evolutionary history of infectious disease and past epidemics.

nodes.label: Domestication
nodes.description: The genomic study of how plant and animal species were brought under human management, tracing selective and demographic signatures of domestication events.

nodes.label: Paleodemography
nodes.description: The reconstruction of past population structure, size, and vital rates from ancient genomic and skeletal evidence.

nodes.label: Medieval and historical-period populations
nodes.description: Genome-wide ancient DNA from Common Era populations — early medieval Britain, Bronze Age-to-Iron Age Aegean, and other historically documented societies — as distinct empirical material from DAG's Paleolithic/Pleistocene work, using written and archaeological record alongside the genomic signal.

provenance.source: curator-drafted; grounded in Gretzinger et al. 2022 Nature (Anglo-Saxon migration) and Skourtanioti et al. 2023 Nature Ecology & Evolution (prehistoric Aegean admixture) — eva.mpg.de/archaeogenetics/

nodes.label: Shotgun sequencing
nodes.description: Untargeted high-throughput sequencing of all DNA fragments in a sample, the default approach for ancient DNA where library content is otherwise unpredictable.

nodes.label: Capture enrichment
nodes.description: A hybridization-based technique that selectively enriches a sequencing library for target genomic regions, used to boost coverage of informative loci from low-yield ancient samples.

nodes.label: Bioinformatics
nodes.description: Computational pipelines for read alignment, quality filtering, damage-pattern authentication, and variant calling that turn raw ancient-DNA sequence data into analyzable genotypes.

nodes.label: Phylogenetics
nodes.description: Methods for reconstructing evolutionary relationships and divergence times among lineages from genetic sequence data.

nodes.label: Coalescent modeling
nodes.description: A statistical framework that models how gene lineages sampled today trace back to shared common ancestors, used to infer demographic history and divergence times from genomic variation.

nodes.label: Haplotype analysis
nodes.description: Analysis of blocks of linked genetic variants inherited together, used to detect admixture, selection, and fine-scale population structure.

nodes.label: Identity-by-descent (IBD) segment analysis
nodes.description: Detection of chromosome segments shared between individuals because they were inherited, unbroken by recombination, from a recent common ancestor — the basis for reconstructing kinship and fine-scale population structure directly from genomes, including low-coverage ancient ones once genotype probabilities are imputed.

provenance.source: curator-drafted; grounded in Ringbauer, Huang, Akbari, Mallick, Olalde, Patterson & Reich (2024, Nature Genetics 56:143-151, doi:10.1038/s41588-023-01582-w)

nodes.label: Neanderthal admixture
nodes.description: Open questions about the timing, geography, and functional consequences of interbreeding between modern humans and Neanderthals, whose genomic traces persist in most present-day non-African populations.

nodes.label: Population structure
nodes.description: How genetic variation is organized across geography and social groups, and how that structure has changed through prehistory and history.

nodes.label: Migration waves
nodes.description: Reconstructing successive episodes of human movement and resettlement — e.g. Out-of-Africa dispersals, Neolithic farming expansions, steppe migrations — from ancient genomic transects.

nodes.label: Selection signals
nodes.description: Genomic signatures left by natural selection acting on specific loci (e.g. lactase persistence, high-altitude adaptation), and how to distinguish them reliably from drift.

nodes.label: Genetic drift
nodes.description: The role of random allele-frequency change, especially in small or bottlenecked populations, in shaping the genomic record independent of selection.

nodes.label: Plague genomics and the source of the Black Death
nodes.description: Reconstructing the phylogeny and geographic origin of Yersinia pestis pandemics directly from ancient DNA recovered from burials — DAG's flagship pathogen-genomics result identified 14th-century Central Asia, not the Black Sea/Crimea, as the source of the strain ancestral to the Black Death's explosive 'Big Bang' diversification.

provenance.source: curator-drafted; grounded in Spyrou, Musralina, Gnecchi Ruscone, Kocher, Borbone, Khartanovich, Buzhilova, Djansugurova, Bos, Kühnert, Haak, Slavin & Krause (2022, Nature 606:718-724, doi:10.1038/s41586-022-04800-3, 'The source of the Black Death in fourteenth-century central Eurasia')

nodes.label: Origins of treponemal disease (syphilis)
nodes.description: The long-running debate over whether syphilis and its relatives (the treponemal diseases) originated in the Old World or the New World, addressed directly with ancient Treponema pallidum genomes rather than historical inference alone.

provenance.source: curator-drafted; grounded in Barquera, Sitter, Kirkpatrick, Ramirez, Kocher, Spyrou, Herbig, Krause & Bos (2024/2025, Nature 640:186-193, doi:10.1038/s41586-024-08515-5, 'Ancient genomes reveal a deep history of Treponema pallidum in the Americas'), which found treponemal disease established in the Americas centuries before European contact

nodes.label: Ancient leprosy (Hansen's disease) in the Americas
nodes.description: Reconstructing the deep history of leprosy-causing bacteria — both the well-known Mycobacterium leprae and the rarer M. lepromatosis — from ancient genomes, distinguishing independently established Old World and New World histories of the disease.

provenance.source: curator-drafted; grounded in Ramirez, Sitter, Översti, Herrera-Soto, Kirkpatrick, Nores & Bos (2025, Nature Ecology & Evolution 9:1685-1693, doi:10.1038/s41559-025-02771-y, '4,000-year-old Mycobacterium lepromatosis genomes from Chile reveal long establishment of Hansen's disease in the Americas')

nodes.label: The Anglo-Saxon migration and early English ancestry
nodes.description: Genome-wide ancient DNA testing how much of early medieval England's population descends from Continental migrants versus existing Romano-British populations, and whether that migration was sex-biased — the first large-scale genomic study of this historically documented but genomically under-tested migration.

provenance.source: curator-drafted; grounded in Gretzinger, Sayer, Justeau, Altena, Pala, Dulias, Edwards, ... Haak, Bos, ... Reich, Krause & Schiffels (2022, Nature 610:112-119, doi:10.1038/s41586-022-05247-2, 'The Anglo-Saxon migration and the formation of the early English gene pool'), finding up to ~76% Continental ancestry in some early medieval English communities plus detectable sex-biased migration

nodes.label: Bronze Age Aegean admixture and endogamy
nodes.description: Fine-grained ancient-DNA reconstruction of population history across Neolithic-to-Iron-Age Crete, mainland Greece, and the Aegean islands, tracing when Anatolian-derived and later steppe-derived ancestry arrived in different parts of the region, and detecting localized endogamy (mating within a small, closed community).

provenance.source: curator-drafted; grounded in Skourtanioti, Ringbauer, Gnecchi Ruscone, Bianco, ... Krause, Jeong & Stockhammer (2023, Nature Ecology & Evolution 7:290-303, doi:10.1038/s41559-022-01952-3, 'Ancient DNA reveals admixture history and endogamy in the prehistoric Aegean')

nodes.label: Kinship and pedigree reconstruction from ancient DNA
nodes.description: Using genome-wide identity-by-descent signal to reconstruct biological relatedness — parent-offspring, sibling, cousin, and more distant kin ties — among individuals buried at the same site, revealing social and family structure that skeletal evidence alone cannot show.

provenance.source: curator-drafted; grounded in Harald Ringbauer's Haplo Group (current DAG research group) and its ancIBD method, and applied directly in this dataset's own fieldsite-issyk-kurgan (Ghalichi, Rohrlach, Gnecchi-Ruscone, Haak & Krause 2026, Science Advances, doi:10.1126/sciadv.aef0108, elite dynastic-lineage reconstruction — first-author attribution corrected 2026-09-03 via live Crossref verification, was previously misattributed to Haak)

nodes.label: Ancient DNA from human ancestral remains
nodes.description: The field has moved, following documented controversies (including cases at MPI-EVA and peer institutions), toward requiring community consultation, consent, and benefit-sharing before ancient-DNA research proceeds on ancestral remains — a 2021 field-wide guidance document (Wagner et al., 'Fostering Responsible Research on Ancient Human Remains,' co-authored by MPI-EVA researchers) sets out the current expected practice.

provenance.source: curator-drafted; grounded in Wagner et al. 2020/2021 'Fostering Responsible Research on Ancient Human Remains' (co-authored by MPI-EVA-affiliated researchers) and documented ancient-DNA consent controversies

nodes.label: Population genetics, ancestry, and 'race' framing
nodes.description: Population genetics is one of the fields most reliably misappropriated to lend false scientific authority to essentialist race concepts, even though the underlying findings (clinal variation, extensive admixture, no genetic basis for discrete race categories) argue directly against that reading.

provenance.source: curator-drafted; grounded in documented field-wide concern (e.g. AAPA statement on race and racism, 2019) about population-genetics misappropriation for race-essentialist claims

nodes.label: 'Percent Neanderthal' popular narratives
nodes.description: Same underlying oversimplification pattern documented under evogen-scicomm-archaic-introgression-headlines, arising here from the demographic-modeling side rather than the functional-genomics side.

provenance.source: curator-drafted; grounded in documented public-communication critiques of consumer ancestry-testing narratives around archaic introgression

nodes.label: Cultural evolution
nodes.description: The theory that culturally transmitted information (skills, beliefs, practices) changes over time through processes analogous to biological evolution — variation, selection, and inheritance via social learning.

nodes.label: Social learning
nodes.description: The study of how individuals acquire information and behavior by observing or interacting with others, rather than through individual trial-and-error.

nodes.label: Cumulative culture
nodes.description: The theory that human culture can accumulate complexity across generations beyond what any single individual could invent alone, via high-fidelity social transmission.

nodes.label: Life history theory
nodes.description: An evolutionary framework explaining how organisms allocate limited resources between growth, reproduction, and survival across the lifespan, shaped by ecological trade-offs.

nodes.label: Cooperation
nodes.description: Theoretical frameworks explaining why individuals incur costs to benefit others, spanning kin selection, reciprocity, and group-level mechanisms.

nodes.label: Kin selection
nodes.description: The theory that helping behavior can evolve when it benefits genetic relatives, formalized by Hamilton's rule relating relatedness, cost, and benefit.

nodes.label: Reciprocity
nodes.description: The theory that cooperation between non-relatives can be sustained through repeated exchange of favors, including direct, indirect, and generalized reciprocity.

nodes.label: Cultural transmission
nodes.description: Formal models of how cultural traits are passed between individuals — vertically (parent to offspring), horizontally (peer to peer), or obliquely — and with what fidelity.

nodes.label: Niche construction
nodes.description: The theory that organisms actively modify their environments in ways that alter the selection pressures acting on themselves and other species, feeding back into evolution.

nodes.label: Behavioral ecology
nodes.description: The study of how behavior is shaped by ecological and social conditions to maximize fitness, using cost-benefit and optimality reasoning.

nodes.label: Evolutionary anthropology
nodes.description: The broad interdisciplinary field applying evolutionary theory to human biology, behavior, and culture, integrating ecology, genetics, and ethnography.

nodes.label: Teaching
nodes.description: The study of costly, other-directed behavior that actively facilitates another individual's learning — theorized as one evolved social-learning strategy among several, distinguished from imitation or observation by the cost it imposes on the teacher and reserved, in practice, for information a learner is unlikely to infer on their own.

provenance.source: curator-drafted; grounded in Boyette & Hewlett (2018, Review of Philosophy and Psychology, 'Teaching in Hunter-Gatherers') and the functional definition of teaching from Caro & Hauser (1992)

nodes.label: Gene-culture coevolution
nodes.description: The theory that genetic and cultural evolution are coupled dynamical processes, each altering the selective conditions the other operates under — e.g. culturally transmitted subsistence practices (like dairying) creating the selection pressure behind a later genetic change (like lactase persistence), or population size and demographic history jointly shaping how much cultural complexity a population can sustain.

provenance.source: curator-drafted; grounded in TICE lab's stated research focus (Fogarty staff profile, eva.mpg.de) and Fogarty, Wakano, Feldman & Aoki (2017, Human Nature, doi:10.1007/s12110-016-9275-6) and Fogarty & Creanza (2017, Phil. Trans. R. Soc. B, doi:10.1098/rstb.2016.0428)

nodes.label: Hunter-gatherers
nodes.description: Contemporary and historically documented foraging societies, a key comparative population for reconstructing ancestral human social and subsistence patterns.

nodes.label: Subsistence strategies
nodes.description: The range of ways human groups obtain food and resources — foraging, pastoralism, horticulture, agriculture — and how these shape social organization.

nodes.label: Foraging
nodes.description: The behavior and decision-making involved in searching for and acquiring wild food resources, studied both ethnographically and through optimal-foraging models.

nodes.label: Mobility patterns
nodes.description: How and why groups move across landscapes — residential and logistical mobility — and its consequences for social structure and resource use.

nodes.label: Demography
nodes.description: The study of population size, structure, fertility, and mortality in small-scale and traditional societies.

nodes.label: Ritual
nodes.description: Formalized, repeated social practices with symbolic content, studied for their role in group cohesion, signaling, and cultural transmission.

nodes.label: Kinship systems
nodes.description: The culturally variable rules and categories that define family relationships, descent, and marriage, and their consequences for cooperation and resource sharing.

nodes.label: Material culture
nodes.description: The physical objects, tools, and artifacts a society produces and uses, studied as evidence of behavior, technology, and cultural transmission.

nodes.label: Innovation
nodes.description: The generation of novel behaviors, tools, or ideas within a population, and the social conditions that favor or suppress it.

nodes.label: Traditions
nodes.description: Behavioral or cultural practices maintained across generations through social learning, studied for their stability, variation, and transmission mechanisms.

nodes.label: Child development
nodes.description: The biocultural study of how children grow, learn, and are cared for — integrating developmental psychology, life history theory, and direct ethnographic observation (focal follows, behavior coding) of everyday learning environments in small-scale societies.

provenance.source: curator-drafted; grounded in Adam Boyette's HBEC research program (Culture, Cooperation and Child Development Research Group) on childhood learning among Aka, Ngandu, and BaYaka communities of the Congo Basin

nodes.label: Arctic Indigenous subsistence economy
nodes.description: Inuit and other Arctic Indigenous foraging, hunting, and harvesting economies, studied for how they interact with an encroaching market/carbon economy — a real, current HBEC field program (the Sanguatsiniq project) distinct from the department's Congo Basin and Pemba Island work.

provenance.source: curator-drafted; grounded in Ready, Ross, Beheim & Parrott (2024, PNAS 121(32), doi:10.1073/pnas.2317686121, 'Indigenous food production in a carbon economy') — eva.mpg.de/ecology/projects-and-research-groups/

nodes.label: Ethnography
nodes.description: Long-term, in-depth qualitative fieldwork documenting the practices, beliefs, and social organization of a community, typically through participant observation.

nodes.label: Field experiments
nodes.description: Controlled behavioral experiments (e.g. economic games) conducted in situ with real communities, combining experimental control with ecological validity.

nodes.label: Agent-based modeling
nodes.description: Computational simulation of populations of interacting individuals following simple rules, used to test how macro-level cultural or social patterns can emerge from micro-level behavior.

nodes.label: Comparative methods
nodes.description: Systematic cross-population or cross-species comparison used to test hypotheses about the causes of behavioral or cultural variation.

nodes.label: Bayesian inference
nodes.description: A statistical framework updating probability estimates for hypotheses as new data arrive, widely used for parameter estimation in behavioral and demographic models.

nodes.label: GIS
nodes.description: Geographic Information Systems used to map, analyze, and model spatial patterns in mobility, resource use, and settlement.

nodes.label: Cross-cultural databases
nodes.description: Large structured datasets coding cultural, social, and ecological variables across many societies, used for statistical cross-cultural comparison (e.g. eHRAF-style resources).

nodes.label: Phylogenetic comparative methods
nodes.description: Statistical techniques that account for shared ancestry between populations or species when testing hypotheses about trait correlations.

nodes.label: Causal inference modeling for cross-cultural comparison
nodes.description: A generative, DAG-based (directed acyclic graph) causal-modeling framework with explicit graphical criteria for deciding when and how findings can be projected or compared across populations, and for formally representing measurement (in)equivalence between societies — distinct from applying a phylogenetic correction, this addresses whether the same construct is even being measured the same way in different cultural contexts.

provenance.source: curator-drafted; grounded in Deffner, Rohrer & McElreath (2022, Advances in Methods and Practices in Psychological Science 5(3):1-18, doi:10.1177/25152459221106366, 'A Causal Framework for Cross-Cultural Generalizability')

nodes.label: Theory-to-data computational workflow
nodes.description: A modeling practice that derives the statistical model used to analyze real field or experimental data directly and transparently from formal cultural-evolution theory, rather than choosing an off-the-shelf statistical test and interpreting it as a theory test after the fact — intended to close a long-standing gap between abstract cultural-evolution models and empirical analysis.

provenance.source: curator-drafted; grounded in Deffner, Fedorova & Andrews & McElreath (2024, PNAS 121(48), doi:10.1073/pnas.2322887121, 'Bridging theory and data: A computational workflow for cultural evolution')

nodes.label: Cooperation
nodes.description: Open questions about the mechanisms and conditions that sustain cooperative behavior in human groups, from small-scale forager bands to large institutions.

nodes.label: Fairness
nodes.description: Cross-cultural and evolutionary study of how norms of fair distribution and exchange emerge, vary, and are enforced.

nodes.label: Punishment
nodes.description: The study of costly sanctioning of norm violators, including third-party and altruistic punishment, and its role in sustaining cooperation.

nodes.label: Partner choice
nodes.description: How individuals select, retain, and switch cooperative partners, and how this market-like dynamic shapes the evolution of cooperative behavior.

nodes.label: Cultural diversity
nodes.description: The patterns, causes, and consequences of variation in beliefs, practices, and institutions across human societies.

nodes.label: Norms
nodes.description: The origins, transmission, and enforcement of shared behavioral expectations within a group.

nodes.label: Institutions
nodes.description: The study of formal and informal rule systems that structure collective action and resource governance in human groups.

nodes.label: Inequality
nodes.description: The evolutionary and ecological origins of resource and status disparities within and between human groups.

nodes.label: Children's play
nodes.description: Cross-cultural and evolutionary study of play — including work-themed and object play — as a low-cost arena where children practice subsistence, social, and motor skills before those skills carry real consequences; a major share of middle childhood's activity budget in small-scale societies.

provenance.source: curator-drafted; grounded in Lew-Levy & Boyette (2018, Human Nature) and Boyette (2016, Child Development)

nodes.label: Socialization of autonomy
nodes.description: How cultural values of personal autonomy and egalitarianism are transmitted to children in practice — for example through task assignment rather than command, and adults' consistent respect for a child's choice to participate, decline, or leave a task.

provenance.source: curator-drafted; grounded in Boyette & Hewlett (2017, Human Nature) and Boyette & Lew-Levy (in press, Ethos, 'The socialization of cooperative autonomy among BaYaka foragers')

nodes.label: Parochial altruism and perceived inequality
nodes.description: Whether in-group-favoring, out-group-costly cooperative behavior ('parochial altruism') is driven mainly by group identity itself or by perceived economic need and inequality — ethnographic, social-network, and economic-game data from two multi-ethnic Colombian communities found perceived group-based economic need explains more of the pattern than identity alone, with high variability both between communities and between individuals.

provenance.source: curator-drafted; grounded in Ross & Pisor (2024/2025, Evolutionary Human Sciences 7, doi:10.1017/ehs.2024.43, 'Perceived inequality and variability in the expression of parochial altruism')

nodes.label: Cross-cultural generalizability
nodes.description: The open methodological question of when a finding from one society can be legitimately compared, pooled, or generalized to another — whether the same construct was actually measured the same way across cultural contexts, not just whether the raw scores differ.

provenance.source: curator-drafted; grounded in Deffner, Rohrer & McElreath (2022, Advances in Methods and Practices in Psychological Science 5(3):1-18, doi:10.1177/25152459221106366)

nodes.label: Ethnographic fieldwork with hunter-gatherer and small-scale societies
nodes.description: Contemporary practice in behavioral ecology and anthropology increasingly requires genuine reciprocity: community consultation on research questions, results shared back in accessible form, and tangible benefit to the community, not just publication credit to the researcher.

provenance.source: curator-drafted; grounded in documented critiques of extractive/parachute fieldwork and calls for reciprocal, consent-based ethnographic practice

nodes.label: 'Living fossil' / timeless-primitive framing of subsistence societies
nodes.description: HBEC's comparative use of subsistence-strategy data to understand human behavioral ecology is scientifically legitimate, but the popular shorthand for why that comparison is useful ('they show us how our ancestors lived') misrepresents living communities as static relics rather than as people living contemporary lives shaped by their own history, including centuries of contact with surrounding states and economies.

provenance.source: curator-drafted; grounded in the anthropological critique of denying coevalness (Fabian, 1983) as applied to popular framings of contemporary hunter-gatherer societies

nodes.label: Language evolution
nodes.description: The study of how human language capacity and individual languages originated and change over time, spanning biological and cultural evolutionary processes.

nodes.label: Cultural evolution
nodes.description: The theory that culturally transmitted traits, including linguistic and narrative traditions, change over generations through variation, selection, and inheritance.

nodes.label: Phylogenetics
nodes.description: The theoretical framework treating languages and cultural traits as lineages that split and diversify, allowing tree-based methods borrowed from evolutionary biology.

nodes.label: Semantic change
nodes.description: The study of how word meanings shift over time, and what regularities (e.g. metaphor, narrowing, broadening) govern that shift across languages.

nodes.label: Linguistic typology
nodes.description: The comparative study of structural diversity and universals across the world's languages, classifying them by grammatical and phonological features.

nodes.label: Social learning
nodes.description: The study of how linguistic and cultural forms are transmitted through observation and interaction rather than innate specification alone.

nodes.label: Language families
nodes.description: Groups of languages descended from a common ancestral language, the basic taxonomic unit for comparative and phylogenetic linguistics.

nodes.label: Lexicons
nodes.description: The vocabulary of a language, used as core comparative data for tracing relatedness, borrowing, and semantic change.

nodes.label: Grammatical structures
nodes.description: The morphological and syntactic rules of languages, compared across families to identify typological patterns and constraints.

nodes.label: Oral traditions
nodes.description: Narratives, histories, and knowledge transmitted verbally across generations, studied as a form of culturally evolving information.

nodes.label: Folklore
nodes.description: Traditional stories, customs, and beliefs of a community, analyzed for patterns of variation, stability, and diffusion.

nodes.label: Mythology
nodes.description: Bodies of traditional narrative, often explaining origins or cosmology, studied comparatively for shared and divergent motifs across cultures.

nodes.label: Cultural traits
nodes.description: Discrete, codeable units of culture (practices, beliefs, technologies) used as the basic data for cultural phylogenetic and comparative analysis.

nodes.label: D-PLACE
nodes.description: The Database of Places, Language, Culture and Environment — a large, curated cross-cultural dataset linking ethnographic, linguistic, environmental, and geographic data for over a thousand human societies, DLCE's flagship comparative resource for testing macro-historical and cultural-evolutionary hypotheses at global scale.

provenance.source: curator-drafted; grounded in eva.mpg.de/linguistic-and-cultural-evolution/research/cool/ (Cultural Evolution) and D-PLACE's own stated role in Chira et al. 2024's 1,000+ mainland societies analysis

nodes.label: Domesticated dogs
nodes.description: Dogs and their human handlers across culturally and ecologically diverse societies, studied both as ethnographic data on human-animal relationships and as a comparative field-experimental population for social cognition, deliberately sampled beyond WEIRD contexts.

provenance.source: curator-drafted; grounded in Chira, Kirby, Epperlein & Bräuer (2023, Scientific Reports, doi:10.1038/s41598-023-31938-5, 124-society cross-cultural dog-use data; DOI Crossref-verified 2026-09-03) and the 5-society hunting-dog field study (Vanuatu, Mongolia, Madagascar, Peru, Germany) described at eva.mpg.de/linguistic-and-cultural-evolution/research/cool/

nodes.label: New Caledonian crows
nodes.description: The only bird species besides humans known to craft hooked tools, and the only phylogenetically independent species with compelling evidence of cumulative technological culture — studied in the wild and in aviaries as a comparative test case for the origins of cumulative technology, distinct from humans' own primate lineage.

provenance.source: curator-drafted; grounded in the Crow Cognition Group (CrowCoG) research program described at eva.mpg.de/linguistic-and-cultural-evolution/research/cool/

nodes.label: Bayesian phylogenetics
nodes.description: Probabilistic tree-inference methods, adapted from evolutionary biology, used to estimate language family trees and divergence dates from lexical or typological data.

nodes.label: Comparative linguistics
nodes.description: The classical method of systematically comparing related languages to reconstruct proto-forms and establish genealogical relationships.

nodes.label: Database construction
nodes.description: Building large, structured, cross-linguistic or cross-cultural datasets that make systematic comparative and statistical analysis possible.

nodes.label: Statistical modeling
nodes.description: Quantitative modeling of patterns in linguistic and cultural data, testing hypotheses about drivers of diversification and change.

nodes.label: Network analysis
nodes.description: Graph-based methods for representing and analyzing contact, borrowing, and influence relationships between languages or cultural traditions that don't fit a strict tree model.

nodes.label: Text mining
nodes.description: Computational extraction of patterns and structure from large bodies of text, used to study semantic change and narrative motifs at scale.

nodes.label: Dynamic co-evolutionary modeling
nodes.description: Phylogenetic comparative models that test whether two traits (e.g. a cultural practice and a form of social organization) changed together over evolutionary time as a coupled dynamical system, distinguishing genuine co-evolution from a correlation that disappears once shared ancestry or spatial non-independence is controlled for.

provenance.source: curator-drafted; grounded in Hrnčíř et al. 2025b's use of 'recently developed dynamic co-evolutionary models' to test kava/sociopolitical-institution co-evolution (eva.mpg.de/linguistic-and-cultural-evolution/research/cool/)

nodes.label: Cross-cultural field experiments
nodes.description: Standardized experimental test batteries and questionnaires administered by researchers in person across multiple, culturally and ecologically diverse field sites, allowing rigorous experimental comparison rather than reliance on ethnographic databases or observational data alone.

provenance.source: curator-drafted; grounded in the 5-society hunting-dog cognition study's 6-experiment social-cognitive test battery plus questionnaire (eva.mpg.de/linguistic-and-cultural-evolution/research/cool/)

nodes.label: Language diversification
nodes.description: How and why languages split and diverge over time, and what social and demographic factors accelerate or slow the process.

nodes.label: Contact-induced change
nodes.description: Linguistic and cultural change resulting from sustained contact between populations, including borrowing, code-switching, and structural convergence.

nodes.label: Cultural phylogenies
nodes.description: Tree-like reconstructions of the history of cultural traits, and the open question of when tree models are appropriate versus when reticulate/network models are needed.

nodes.label: Co-evolution of language and culture
nodes.description: The extent to which linguistic diversification tracks, or diverges from, broader cultural and population history.

nodes.label: Semantic universals
nodes.description: Whether there are recurring, cross-linguistically stable patterns in how meanings are organized and how they shift over time.

nodes.label: Testing macro-historical hypotheses
nodes.description: Subjecting influential 'big-history' narratives about the human past — such as Jared Diamond's axis-of-orientation hypothesis that Eurasia's east-west geography facilitated cultural diffusion — to quantitative testing with large comparative cultural, linguistic, ecological, and archaeological datasets, rather than treating them as settled narrative.

provenance.source: curator-drafted; grounded in Chira, Gray & Botero (2024, Evolutionary Human Sciences, 6: e5, doi:10.1017/ehs.2023.34, 'Geography is not destiny: A quantitative test of Diamond's axis of orientation hypothesis'), which found ecological barriers do inhibit cultural transmission but Eurasia is not more environmentally homogeneous than other continents — DOI added and Crossref-verified 2026-09-03

nodes.label: Intoxicants and sociopolitical complexity
nodes.description: Whether traditional intoxicants (alcohol, kava) played a causal role in the emergence and maintenance of complex societies, tested against the alternative that agricultural intensity, environmental productivity, and spatial non-independence better explain any observed association.

provenance.source: curator-drafted; grounded in Hrnčíř, Chira & Gray (2025, Humanities and Social Sciences Communications, doi:10.1057/s41599-025-05503-6, 'Did alcohol facilitate the evolution of complex societies?' — 186 societies: alcohol-political complexity association modest once agriculture/productivity controlled; DOI found and Crossref-verified 2026-09-03, correcting this node's earlier untraced 'Hrnčíř et al. 2025a' placeholder citation — actual venue is Humanities and Social Sciences Communications, not the same journal as the companion kava paper) and Hrnčíř, Sheehan, Claessens & Gray (2026, PNAS, doi:10.1073/pnas.2521658123, 'Kava consumption and the rise of sociopolitical complexity in Oceania' — 83 Oceanic societies: kava-complexity correlation disappears once spatial non-independence controlled; dynamic co-evolutionary models find no evidence kava and sociopolitical institutions evolved together; published year is 2026, not 2025 as this node's own label suggested — Crossref-verified 2026-09-03, a 2025 OSF preprint of the same title also exists, doi:10.31235/osf.io/mcbdk_v1) — eva.mpg.de/linguistic-and-cultural-evolution/research/cool/

nodes.label: Human-dog relationships across cultures
nodes.description: How the dog-human bond varies and stays stable across culturally and ecologically diverse societies — both the ethnographic record of dog use, care, and treatment, and direct cross-cultural experimental comparison of dog-owner social cognition, addressing a WEIRD bias in animal cognition research that mirrors the one long noted in human psychology.

provenance.source: curator-drafted; grounded in Chira, Kirby, Epperlein & Bräuer (2023, Scientific Reports, doi:10.1038/s41598-023-31938-5, 'Function predicts how people treat their dogs in a global sample' — 124 societies: closer human-dog relationships linked to multifunctional roles — hunting, guarding, herding — with positive care and harsh treatment frequently co-occurring; DOI Crossref-verified 2026-09-03) and the 5-society hunting-dog cognition field study (Vanuatu, Mongolia, Madagascar, Peru, Germany: striking cross-cultural similarity in dog-human social-cognitive bonds) — eva.mpg.de/linguistic-and-cultural-evolution/research/cool/

nodes.label: Cumulative technological culture in New Caledonian crows
nodes.description: What traits enable cumulative technological culture to emerge, studied through the only phylogenetically independent non-human species with compelling evidence of it — combining field censuses of tool designs and their social/asocial learning contexts with aviary experiments on the (a)social learning mechanisms and cognitive abilities (e.g. probabilistic inference, overhypothesis formation) that support them.

provenance.source: curator-drafted; grounded in the Crow Cognition Group (CrowCoG) research program's documented geographic diversity in tool designs, potential generational nut-dropping styles, and cognitive mechanisms — eva.mpg.de/linguistic-and-cultural-evolution/research/cool/

nodes.label: Evolution of religious diversity
nodes.description: Phylogenetic and comparative reconstruction of how global religious diversity arose and diversified, testing specific historical hypotheses about the deep structure of that diversification rather than treating it as a single, uniform process.

provenance.source: curator-drafted; grounded in Ejova, Sheehan, Bouckaert, Greenhill, Krátký, Kotherová, Cigán, Kundtová Klocová, Kundt, Watts, Bulbulia, Atkinson & Gray (2025, Evolutionary Human Sciences, 7: e43, doi:10.1017/ehs.2025.10027, 'Three evolutionary radiations shaped the evolution of global religious diversity') — DOI added and Crossref-verified 2026-09-03

nodes.label: Indo-European homeland debate
nodes.description: Where and when the Indo-European language family originated and spread — the long-running contest between an Anatolian farming-expansion origin (~9,500 years ago) and a Pontic-Caspian steppe-migration origin (~6,000 years ago), tested with Bayesian linguistic phylogenetics and, more recently, reconciled against ancient-DNA migration evidence rather than settled by either dataset alone.

provenance.source: curator-drafted; grounded in Bouckaert, Lemey, Dunn, Greenhill, Alekseyenko, Drummond, Gray, Suchard & Atkinson (2012, Science, doi:10.1126/science.1219669, 'Mapping the Origins and Expansion of the Indo-European Language Family' — Bayesian phylogeography supporting an Anatolian origin), Haak et al. (2015, Nature, doi:10.1038/nature14317, 'Massive migration from the steppe was a source for Indo-European languages in Europe' — ancient-DNA evidence for steppe migration), and Heggarty, Anderson, Scarborough, King, Bouckaert et al. (2023, Science, doi:10.1126/science.abg0818, 'Language trees with sampled ancestors support a hybrid model for the origin of Indo-European languages' — 162-language IE-CoR dataset, hybrid model: homeland south of the Caucasus with a branch onto the Pontic-Caspian steppe, reconciling both hypotheses; all three DOIs Crossref-verified 2026-09-03) — the same real science already underlying this repo's live `dlce-indoeuropean` whiteboard module, see docs/dlce-geographic-diversity-and-research-frames.md

nodes.label: Genetic-linguistic population correlation
nodes.description: Whether population-genetic structure and linguistic-family structure track the same underlying population history, and where they diverge — e.g. language shift without population replacement, or population replacement without language shift — a comparative program spanning population genetics, archaeology, and historical linguistics since its founding synthesis.

provenance.source: curator-drafted; grounded in Cavalli-Sforza, Piazza, Menozzi & Mountain (1988, PNAS, doi:10.1073/pnas.85.16.6002, 'Reconstruction of human evolution: bringing together genetic, archaeological, and linguistic data' — DOI added and Crossref-verified 2026-09-03), the founding paper of this comparative genetic-linguistic program, which DLCE's own dlce-topic-coevolution-of-language-and-culture continues in updated form

nodes.label: Genetic basis of language capacity
nodes.description: The genetic and molecular substrate of the human capacity for speech and language, and when in human evolution it arose — most prominently studied through FOXP2, a gene whose disruption causes a severe inherited speech/language disorder and whose human-specific amino-acid changes show a molecular signature of positive selection.

provenance.source: curator-drafted; grounded in Lai, Fisher, Hurst, Vargha-Khadem & Monaco (2001, Nature, doi:10.1038/35097076, FOXP2 mutation causing the KE family's speech/language disorder), Enard, Przeworski, Fisher, Lai, Wiebe, Kitano, Monaco & Pääbo (2002, Nature, doi:10.1038/nature01025, human-specific FOXP2 substitutions bearing a signature of positive selection), and Krause, Lalueza-Fox, Orlando, Enard, Green, Burbano, Hublin, Hänni, Fortea, de la Rasilla, Bertranpetit, Rosas & Pääbo (2007, Current Biology, doi:10.1016/j.cub.2007.10.008, 'The Derived FOXP2 Variant of Modern Humans Was Shared with Neandertals' — all three DOIs Crossref-verified 2026-09-03)

nodes.label: Documentation of endangered and minority languages
nodes.description: Language documentation data (recordings, transcriptions, dictionaries) is a form of community cultural heritage, not just raw research material — leading practice treats speakers as knowledge-holders and partners in what gets documented, archived, and made public, not just as data sources.

provenance.source: curator-drafted; grounded in documented community-based language-documentation ethics practice (e.g. community-controlled archiving standards used in language-revitalization work)

nodes.label: 'Language death' deficit framing
nodes.description: DLCE's research on language diversification and contact-induced change documents real, often externally-driven pressures on minority languages, but the standard media vocabulary for describing this ('endangered,' 'dying,' 'extinct') was itself developed in a way some linguists and communities now consider to import a biological-extinction metaphor that doesn't fit how communities themselves experience language shift and revitalization.

provenance.source: curator-drafted; grounded in documented critiques of biological-extinction metaphors in endangered-language discourse within linguistics

nodes.label: Molecular evolution
nodes.description: The study of how DNA, RNA, and protein sequences change over evolutionary time, and the mechanisms (mutation, selection, drift) that drive those changes.

nodes.label: Population genetics
nodes.description: The mathematical theory of how allele and genotype frequencies change within populations under mutation, selection, drift, and migration.

nodes.label: Neutral theory
nodes.description: Kimura's theory that most molecular-level evolutionary change is driven by random drift of selectively neutral or nearly-neutral mutations, not positive selection.

nodes.label: Selection and drift
nodes.description: The interplay between deterministic natural selection and stochastic genetic drift in shaping allele frequency trajectories, especially in small populations.

nodes.label: Coalescent theory
nodes.description: A retrospective model of how gene lineages sampled from a population trace back to common ancestors, foundational for inferring demographic and selective history from genomic data.

nodes.label: Mutation-selection balance
nodes.description: The equilibrium reached when new deleterious mutations entering a population are balanced by selection removing them, used to explain persistence of disease alleles.

nodes.label: Evolutionary genomics
nodes.description: The genome-wide study of evolutionary processes, integrating population genetics theory with large-scale sequencing data.

nodes.label: Modern human genomes
nodes.description: Present-day human genomic sequence data, used as the baseline for detecting selection, admixture, and functional variation.

nodes.label: Archaic hominin genomes
nodes.description: Genomic sequences recovered from Neanderthals, Denisovans, and other archaic hominins, used to reconstruct their biology and legacy in modern humans.

nodes.label: Comparative primate genomics
nodes.description: Cross-species comparison of primate genomes to identify human-specific and lineage-specific genomic changes.

nodes.label: Functional genomics
nodes.description: The study of gene and genome function — expression, regulation, and molecular activity — beyond sequence alone.

nodes.label: Regulatory elements
nodes.description: Non-coding genomic sequences (promoters, enhancers) that control when and where genes are expressed, an important substrate for evolutionary change.

nodes.label: Mitochondrial DNA
nodes.description: Maternally inherited genetic material used for tracing matrilineal ancestry and population history due to its high copy number and lack of recombination.

nodes.label: Y-chromosome variation
nodes.description: Patrilineally inherited genetic variation used for tracing paternal ancestry and population history.

nodes.label: Whole-genome sequencing
nodes.description: Sequencing of an organism's entire genome, providing comprehensive coverage for evolutionary and functional analysis.

nodes.label: Exome sequencing
nodes.description: Targeted sequencing of only the protein-coding regions of the genome, a cost-effective way to focus on functionally interpretable variation.

nodes.label: Genotype imputation
nodes.description: Statistical inference of unobserved genotypes using a reference panel of haplotypes, extending the value of sparser genotyping data.

nodes.label: Haplotype-based inference
nodes.description: Analysis of linked variant combinations inherited together, used to detect selection, admixture, and recent demographic events.

nodes.label: Selection scans
nodes.description: Genome-wide statistical tests that identify regions bearing the signature of past natural selection.

nodes.label: Linkage disequilibrium analysis
nodes.description: Analysis of non-random association between alleles at different loci, informative about recombination history, selection, and population structure.

nodes.label: Phylogenomic analysis
nodes.description: Reconstruction of evolutionary relationships using genome-scale sequence data rather than single genes or markers.

nodes.label: Functional annotation
nodes.description: Computational and experimental assignment of biological function to genomic regions and variants.

nodes.label: Expression quantitative trait loci
nodes.description: Genomic loci (eQTLs) statistically associated with variation in gene expression levels, linking genotype to regulatory phenotype.

nodes.label: CRISPR-based archaic-allele reversion
nodes.description: Genome-editing technique that reverts modern human stem-cell DNA to the ancestral or archaic (Neanderthal/Denisovan) state at one specific site, creating 'Neandertalized' cell lines that isolate the functional effect of a single human-specific genetic change from the rest of the genome.

provenance.source: curator-drafted; grounded in Stephan Riesenberg's Genome Engineering and Repair group, eva.mpg.de/genetics/

nodes.label: Introgression from archaic hominins
nodes.description: The functional and phenotypic consequences of Neanderthal- and Denisovan-derived genetic variants persisting in modern human genomes.

nodes.label: Adaptive evolution
nodes.description: Identifying and characterizing genomic regions that have been shaped by positive selection in human or primate lineages.

nodes.label: Disease-associated variants
nodes.description: The evolutionary origins and population-frequency dynamics of genetic variants linked to disease risk.

nodes.label: Demographic bottlenecks
nodes.description: Episodes of sharp population-size reduction inferred from genomic diversity patterns, and their long-term effects on genetic variation.

nodes.label: Effective population size
nodes.description: The idealized population size that would produce the observed level of genetic drift, a key parameter for interpreting diversity and selection.

nodes.label: Genetic load
nodes.description: The accumulated burden of deleterious mutations in a population or genome, and how it varies with demographic history and inbreeding.

nodes.label: Evolution of gene regulation
nodes.description: How changes in regulatory sequence and expression, rather than protein-coding sequence, have contributed to phenotypic evolution.

nodes.label: Comparative genomics of primates
nodes.description: Identifying genomic changes unique to specific primate lineages, including humans, to understand the genetic basis of lineage-specific traits.

nodes.label: Neanderthal-introgressed COVID-19 risk and protective haplotypes
nodes.description: Two distinct Neanderthal-derived genomic regions with opposite, clinically real effects on COVID-19 severity in living carriers: a chromosome-3 haplotype (near CXCR6/LZTFL1) substantially raising risk of severe disease, and a chromosome-12 haplotype (the OAS gene cluster) associated with reduced risk — the clearest contemporary-health case of archaic introgression's ongoing functional relevance.

provenance.source: curator-drafted; grounded in Zeberg & Pääbo (2020, Nature 587:610-612, doi:10.1038/s41586-020-2818-3) and Zeberg & Pääbo (2021, PNAS 118(9):e2026309118, doi:10.1073/pnas.2026309118)

nodes.label: Archaic Y-chromosome and mtDNA replacement
nodes.description: Both the Y chromosome and mitochondrial DNA of Neanderthals appear to have been replaced by early-modern-human-derived versions via gene flow roughly 100,000-370,000 years ago — a distinct, earlier and more complete replacement pattern than the partial autosomal admixture that left most living non-Africans with Neanderthal ancestry.

provenance.source: curator-drafted; grounded in Petr, Hajdinjak, Fu, Essel, Rougier, Crevecoeur, et al. & Kelso (2020, Science 369(6511):1653-1656, doi:10.1126/science.abb6460, 'The evolutionary history of Neanderthal and Denisovan Y chromosomes')

nodes.label: Timing of the single major Neanderthal admixture pulse
nodes.description: Genomes from ~45,000-year-old modern humans show Neanderthal ancestry segments tracing to one shared admixture event, refining when interbreeding actually happened — roughly 45,000-49,000 years ago, in a window estimated to have lasted about 7,000 years — rather than a vaguer 'sometime after leaving Africa' estimate.

provenance.source: curator-drafted; grounded in Sümer, Rougier, Villalba-Mouco, et al., Kelso, Zeberg, ..., Peter, Meyer, ..., Hajdinjak, Prüfer & Krause (2024, Nature, doi:10.1038/s41586-024-08420-x, 'Earliest modern human genomes constrain timing of Neanderthal admixture')

nodes.label: Neanderthal introgression and pain sensitivity
nodes.description: Three Neanderthal-introgressed missense variants in SCN9A, the gene encoding the pain channel Nav1.7, are associated with a lower mechanical pain threshold after sensitization in a modern human cohort — a concrete example connecting archaic introgression to a specific, testable physiological trait rather than a diffuse behavioral claim.

provenance.source: curator-drafted; grounded in Zeberg et al., incl. Pääbo (2023, Communications Biology 6:981, doi:10.1038/s42003-023-05286-z, 'Neanderthal introgression in SCN9A impacts mechanical pain sensitivity')

nodes.label: Functional validation of archaic-derived genetic variants
nodes.description: Testing what a specific human-specific or archaic-introgressed genetic change actually does — via CRISPR-based reversion of modern human stem cells to the ancestral/archaic state (Stephan Riesenberg's Genome Engineering and Repair group) — and, just as importantly, critically re-examining other labs' functional claims when the underlying cell lines or methods don't support them.

provenance.source: curator-drafted; grounded in Stephan Riesenberg's Genome Engineering and Repair group (current EvoGen research group, eva.mpg.de/genetics/) and Maricic, Riesenberg & Pääbo (2021, Science 374:eabi6060, doi:10.1126/science.abi6060)

nodes.label: Mouse models for functional validation of human-evolutionary variants
nodes.description: This is standard, tightly regulated animal-research practice used to test what a genetic difference actually does, but 'putting a human gene variant into a mouse' is exactly the kind of phrase that reads very differently to a lay audience than to a geneticist.

provenance.source: curator-drafted; grounded in documented functional genomics practice using mouse models to test human-specific and archaic-introgressed regulatory variants

nodes.label: Disease-associated variants and population framing
nodes.description: EvoGen's work on disease-associated variants and genetic load is about population history and molecular mechanism, not about ranking populations, but the distinction is exactly what gets lost when a finding is compressed into a headline.

provenance.source: curator-drafted; grounded in documented critiques of genetic-determinist and racialized misreadings of population-genetics findings

nodes.label: 'Percent Neanderthal' popular narratives
nodes.description: EvoGen studies the functional and phenotypic consequences of specific introgressed variants — most of the archaic-derived genome has no known effect at all — but public narratives tend to treat 'percent archaic ancestry' itself as the meaningful finding.

provenance.source: curator-drafted; grounded in documented public-communication critiques of consumer ancestry-testing narratives around archaic introgression

nodes.label: Genomic sampling of diverse global populations
nodes.description: EvoGen's population-genomics work depends on this kind of broad sampling to represent real human genetic diversity rather than over-relying on already-oversampled populations, which is itself a scientific-quality and equity issue, not just an ethics add-on.

provenance.source: curator-drafted; grounded in the documented Havasupai Tribe genomic-consent case and broader calls for equitable, diverse genomic reference panels

nodes.label: Hominin evolution
nodes.description: The broad evolutionary account of the lineage leading to modern humans, spanning multiple extinct hominin species and their relationships.

nodes.label: Life history evolution
nodes.description: How the timing of growth, maturation, and reproduction evolved across hominin lineages, inferred from skeletal and dental developmental evidence.

nodes.label: Paleoanthropology
nodes.description: The broader discipline studying human evolution through fossil, archaeological, and comparative anatomical evidence.

nodes.label: Evolutionary morphology
nodes.description: The study of how anatomical form has changed over evolutionary time in response to functional and developmental constraints.

nodes.label: Adaptation
nodes.description: The theory that anatomical and behavioral traits evolve in response to selective pressures from the environment and way of life.

nodes.label: Biomechanics
nodes.description: The application of mechanical principles to understand how skeletal form relates to movement and function, e.g. in reconstructing locomotion from fossil bones.

nodes.label: Fossil hominins
nodes.description: Skeletal and dental remains of extinct members of the human lineage, the primary physical evidence for reconstructing human evolutionary history.

nodes.label: Paleoenvironments
nodes.description: Reconstructions of past climates, landscapes, and ecosystems that hominins inhabited, used to contextualize evolutionary and behavioral change.

nodes.label: Stone tools
nodes.description: Lithic artifacts produced by hominins, used as evidence for cognitive, behavioral, and technological evolution.

nodes.label: Skeletal morphology
nodes.description: The form and structure of bones, analyzed comparatively across hominin species to reconstruct locomotion, body size, and life history.

nodes.label: Dental evolution
nodes.description: Changes in tooth form, wear, and development across hominin lineages, informative about diet, growth rate, and taxonomy.

nodes.label: Paleogenomics
nodes.description: Ancient genomic evidence integrated with fossil and archaeological data to address questions about hominin origins and relationships.

nodes.label: Geometric morphometrics
nodes.description: Quantitative analysis of shape using coordinates of anatomical landmarks, allowing statistical comparison of skeletal form across specimens and species.

nodes.label: CT scanning
nodes.description: Computed tomography imaging used to non-destructively visualize internal bone and dental structure in fossil specimens.

nodes.label: 3D reconstruction
nodes.description: Digital modeling of fragmentary or distorted fossil remains into complete three-dimensional forms for analysis.

nodes.label: Stable isotopes
nodes.description: Chemical analysis of isotope ratios in bones and teeth used to reconstruct diet, mobility, and environment.

nodes.label: Paleoecology
nodes.description: Reconstruction of past ecological relationships and habitats from fossil and sedimentary evidence.

nodes.label: Taphonomy
nodes.description: The study of what happens to organic remains between death and fossilization/discovery, essential for correctly interpreting the fossil record.

nodes.label: Radiocarbon dating
nodes.description: Radiometric dating of organic material based on carbon-14 decay, used to establish chronologies for sites within its ~50,000-year range.

nodes.label: Proteomics
nodes.description: Analysis of ancient proteins preserved in fossils, useful for taxonomic identification and phylogenetic placement when DNA is not preserved.

nodes.label: Trabecular and cortical bone microstructure analysis
nodes.description: MicroCT-based quantification of a bone's internal architecture — the density and orientation of spongy trabecular bone, and the thickness of dense cortical bone — used as a functional signal of how a limb or digit was actually loaded and used during life, distinct from and complementary to external shape (geometric morphometrics).

provenance.source: curator-drafted; grounded in Tracy Kivell's research program (eva.mpg.de/human-origins/staff/tracy-kivell/) and Bird, Kivell, Dunmore & Skinner (2023, American Journal of Biological Anthropology, doi:10.1002/ajpa.24824)

nodes.label: Controlled experimental replication
nodes.description: Actualistic experiments that reproduce a candidate archaeological signature under controlled, known conditions — e.g. trampling flint flakes on measured substrates to see what edge damage results — so that a real archaeological pattern can be tested against a known-cause baseline rather than interpreted on typological grounds alone.

provenance.source: curator-drafted; grounded in McPherron, Braun, Dogandžić, Archer, Desta & Lin (2014, Journal of Archaeological Science 49:70-82, doi:10.1016/j.jas.2014.04.003) — DOI verified live via literaturebase_verify_doi

nodes.label: Bipedalism
nodes.description: The evolutionary origins and biomechanical consequences of habitual upright, two-legged locomotion, a defining hominin trait.

nodes.label: Diet reconstruction
nodes.description: Inferring what extinct hominins ate from dental wear, isotopes, and associated archaeological evidence.

nodes.label: Growth and development
nodes.description: How the pace and pattern of skeletal and dental maturation evolved across hominin species, and what it implies about life history.

nodes.label: Climate adaptation
nodes.description: How hominin anatomy and behavior adapted to changing and variable Pleistocene climates.

nodes.label: Migration
nodes.description: The dispersal of hominin species out of and across continents, reconstructed from fossil and archaeological distributions.

nodes.label: Archaic humans
nodes.description: The biology, behavior, and relationships of non-modern Homo populations such as Neanderthals, Denisovans, and Homo erectus.

nodes.label: Evolution of manual dexterity and grip
nodes.description: How hominin hand and thumb capability for precise manipulation evolved, assessed through internal bone structure (which tracks how a bone was actually loaded in life) rather than tool assemblages alone — current evidence shows dexterity evolved gradually and unevenly rather than as a single clean transition: Australopithecus sediba's thumb and pinky already show human-like manipulation loading while its other fingers remain ape-like and climbing-adapted.

provenance.source: curator-drafted; grounded in Syeda, Kivell et al. (2025, Science Advances 11, doi:10.1126/sciadv.adt1201, 'Phalangeal cortical bone distribution reveals different dexterous and climbing behaviors in Australopithecus sediba and Homo naledi') and Dunmore, Kivell, Skinner et al. (2024, American Journal of Biological Anthropology, doi:10.1002/ajpa.24695)

nodes.label: The Sahelanthropus bipedalism debate
nodes.description: An open, actively contested question of whether Sahelanthropus tchadensis (c. 7 million years old, among the oldest putative hominins) walked habitually upright — a 2022 study argued yes from external femur/postcrania morphology, while a 2024 re-analysis incorporating internal (trabecular) bone structure found no consistent evidence for habitual bipedalism, illustrating how contested even foundational claims about hominin origins remain and how internal bone evidence can adjudicate between competing readings of the same fossils.

provenance.source: curator-drafted; grounded in Cazenave, Pina, Hammond, et al. & Wood (2024, Journal of Human Evolution, doi:10.1016/j.jhevol.2024.103557, 'Postcranial evidence does not support habitual bipedalism in Sahelanthropus tchadensis: A reply to Daver et al. 2022')

nodes.label: Taphonomy vs. intentional modification
nodes.description: Distinguishing genuine hominin-made cut marks, percussion marks, and tool retouch from damage produced by natural post-depositional processes — trampling, sediment compaction, carnivore gnawing — that can closely mimic intentional modification. A methodological problem with direct stakes for how far back stone-tool use and butchery can be confidently claimed.

provenance.source: curator-drafted; grounded in McPherron, Alemseged, Marean, Wynn, Reed, Geraads, Bobe & Béarat (2010, Nature, doi:10.1038/nature09248, 'Evidence for stone-tool-assisted consumption of animal tissues before 3.39 million years ago at Dikika, Ethiopia') and McPherron, Braun, Dogandžić, Archer, Desta & Lin (2014, Journal of Archaeological Science 49:70-82, doi:10.1016/j.jas.2014.04.003, controlled trampling/edge-damage replication experiments) — both DOIs verified live via literaturebase_verify_doi

nodes.label: Fossil hominin collections with colonial-era acquisition histories
nodes.description: Contemporary practice increasingly requires genuine host-country partnership (co-authorship, capacity building, specimens remaining in or returning to the country of origin) rather than the older extractive model where fossils traveled to European or North American institutions and host-country researchers did not.

provenance.source: curator-drafted; grounded in documented critiques of colonial-era paleoanthropological collecting practice and calls for host-country research partnership

nodes.label: 'Missing link' and linear-progress narratives
nodes.description: HumOr's own research on hominin diversity, archaic humans, and coexisting lineages directly contradicts the linear-progress image, but that image is so culturally entrenched that it resurfaces by default unless exhibit and press copy actively work against it.

provenance.source: curator-drafted; grounded in well-documented critiques of the 'March of Progress' image and linear human-evolution narratives in science communication and museum studies

nodes.label: Primate social evolution
nodes.description: The study of how social organization, group living, and social bonds evolved across primate species in response to ecological and reproductive pressures.

nodes.label: Life history theory
nodes.description: An evolutionary framework explaining how primates allocate resources between growth, reproduction, and survival across the lifespan.

nodes.label: Behavioral ecology
nodes.description: The study of how primate behavior is shaped by ecological conditions such as food distribution, predation risk, and habitat structure to maximize fitness.

nodes.label: Social network theory
nodes.description: A framework for representing and analyzing the structure of social relationships within a group as a network of connections, used to study bonds, hierarchy, and information flow.

nodes.label: Cooperation and conflict
nodes.description: Theoretical frameworks explaining when primates cooperate versus compete, including coalition formation and conflict resolution.

nodes.label: Sexual selection
nodes.description: The theory that traits can evolve because they increase mating success rather than survival, shaping primate mating systems, ornamentation, and competition.

nodes.label: Parental investment
nodes.description: Trivers' theory that the sex investing more in offspring becomes the choosier sex, shaping mating systems and parental care patterns across primates.

nodes.label: Wild primate populations
nodes.description: Free-ranging, non-captive primate groups studied in their natural habitats, providing ecologically valid behavioral data.

nodes.label: Baboons
nodes.description: Old World monkeys widely studied as a model for understanding primate social structure, stress physiology, and life history under variable ecological conditions.

nodes.label: Chimpanzees
nodes.description: Humans' closest living relatives, extensively studied for insight into the evolutionary origins of cooperation, culture, and cognition.

nodes.label: Monkeys
nodes.description: Old and New World monkey species studied comparatively across the primate order for insight into the diversity of social and reproductive strategies.

nodes.label: Social groups
nodes.description: The composition, size, and organization of primate social units, studied for their ecological and evolutionary drivers.

nodes.label: Dominance hierarchies
nodes.description: Rank-ordered systems of social status within primate groups that shape access to resources, mates, and social support.

nodes.label: Mating systems
nodes.description: The patterns of sexual pairing (monogamy, polygyny, promiscuity) observed across primate species and their ecological correlates.

nodes.label: Dispersal
nodes.description: The movement of individuals away from their natal group, a key process shaping gene flow, social structure, and inbreeding avoidance.

nodes.label: Kinship
nodes.description: Genetic relatedness among group members and its influence on cooperative and competitive social behavior.

nodes.label: Gorillas
nodes.description: Wild gorilla populations, studied for social organization, sociality, and — via the department's Social Microbiome group — gut microbiome variation shaped by social group membership and host ecology rather than diet or phylogeny alone.

provenance.source: curator-drafted; grounded in Martha Robbins' Gorilla Group, a current PrimEvo research group (eva.mpg.de/primate-behavior-and-evolution/)

nodes.label: Pan-African chimpanzee populations
nodes.description: Chimpanzee populations sampled across all four Pan troglodytes subspecies at over 40 field sites in roughly 15 African countries — a deliberately cross-sectional, breadth-over-depth research design (the Pan African Programme: The Cultured Chimpanzee, PanAf) that complements this department's deep single-site studies (Taï, Amboseli) by comparing many populations' ecology and behavior simultaneously rather than following one population for decades.

provenance.source: curator-drafted; grounded in Kalan, Kulik, Arandjelovic, Boesch, Haas, Dieguez et al. & Kühl (2020, Nature Communications, doi:10.1038/s41467-020-18176-3) and panafrican.eva.mpg.de's own stated ~35-40-population, cross-sectional design

nodes.label: Long-term field observation
nodes.description: Multi-year, often multi-decade, systematic observation of habituated wild primate groups, enabling life-history and longitudinal social analysis.

nodes.label: Behavioral sampling
nodes.description: Standardized protocols (e.g. focal-animal, scan sampling) for systematically recording behavior to enable quantitative comparison.

nodes.label: Social network analysis
nodes.description: Quantitative analysis of patterns of social interaction as network graphs, used to study bond structure, centrality, and information flow.

nodes.label: Endocrinology and hormones
nodes.description: Measurement of hormone levels (e.g. cortisol, testosterone) from non-invasive samples to study stress, reproduction, and social status.

nodes.label: Genetic relatedness analysis
nodes.description: Molecular methods for determining kinship among group members, used to test how relatedness shapes cooperation and social preference.

nodes.label: GPS tracking
nodes.description: Satellite-based tracking of individual or group movement, used to study ranging patterns, habitat use, and dispersal.

nodes.label: Remote sensing of habitats
nodes.description: Satellite and aerial imagery used to characterize vegetation, resource availability, and habitat change relevant to primate ecology.

nodes.label: Health and parasite monitoring
nodes.description: Systematic assessment of disease, injury, and parasite load in wild primates, linked to social behavior, stress, and life-history outcomes.

nodes.label: Camera-trap video with citizen-science annotation
nodes.description: Remote, unmanned camera traps deployed across many chimpanzee field sites simultaneously, generating thousands of hours of video too large for any one research team to review — annotated instead by public volunteers through the Chimp&See online citizen-science platform (identifying individuals, behaviors, and tool use), enabling behavioral comparison across dozens of populations at once rather than one deeply-studied site at a time.

provenance.source: curator-drafted; grounded in Arandjelovic, Stephens, McCarthy, Dieguez, Kalan, Maldonado, Boesch & Kuehl (2016, PeerJ Preprints, doi:10.7287/peerj.preprints.1792v1, 'Chimp&See: an online citizen science platform for large-scale, remote video camera trap annotation of chimpanzee behaviour, demography and individual identification') and McCarthy, Stephens, Dieguez, Samuni, Després-Einspenner, et al., Wittig, Boesch, Kühl & Arandjelovic (2021, Ecology and Evolution, doi:10.1002/ece3.7128, applying the platform to real individual-identification and social-network data); DOIs Crossref-verified 2026-09-04

nodes.label: Primate archaeology (excavation of living tool-use sites)
nodes.description: Standard archaeological excavation and lithic-analysis techniques (systematic recovery, use-wear and flake-scar analysis) applied to the stone-tool-use sites of living, observable wild primates rather than only to the fossil archaeological record, allowing a directly known toolmaker and known behavior to be compared against the resulting artifact assemblage.

provenance.source: curator-drafted; grounded in Proffitt, Luncz, Falótico, Ottoni, de la Torre & Haslam (2016, Nature, doi:10.1038/nature20112) and Luncz, Gill, Proffitt, Svensson, Kulik & Malaivijitnond (2019, eLife, doi:10.7554/eLife.46961) — both DOIs verified live via literaturebase_verify_doi

nodes.label: Social bonds and fitness
nodes.description: Evidence that strong, stable social relationships causally improve survival and reproductive success in primates.

nodes.label: Cooperation and alliances
nodes.description: How and why primates form coalitions and cooperative alliances, and what maintains them over time.

nodes.label: Reproductive strategies
nodes.description: The diversity of strategies primates use to maximize reproductive success given their mating system, rank, and ecology.

nodes.label: Stress and health
nodes.description: How social and ecological stressors affect physiological stress markers and health outcomes in wild primates.

nodes.label: Early life adversity
nodes.description: The long-term consequences of adverse early-life experiences (maternal loss, low rank, drought) on adult social behavior and fitness.

nodes.label: Gene–environment interactions
nodes.description: How genetic variation and environmental/social conditions jointly shape primate behavior and life-history outcomes.

nodes.label: Social structure and demography
nodes.description: How group size, sex ratio, and age structure interact with social organization over time.

nodes.label: Cultural traditions in primates
nodes.description: Socially learned, group-specific behavioral traditions (e.g. tool use variants) documented in wild primate populations, relevant to debates about the evolutionary origins of culture.

nodes.label: Biological embedding of early-life adversity
nodes.description: How environmental and social hardship in infancy leaves lasting molecular signatures — measured here as DNA-methylation patterns at hundreds of thousands of genomic sites — shaping adult health and lifespan. In wild Amboseli baboons, resource-limitation exposures (poor habitat quality, early-life drought) left far stronger, more compounding methylation signatures than social adversity (maternal loss, low rank, social isolation), challenging assumptions that social stress is the dominant embedding pathway.

provenance.source: curator-drafted; grounded in Anderson, Lin, Lea, Johnston, Voyles, Akinyi, Archie, Alberts & Tung (2024, PNAS 121(11), doi:10.1073/pnas.2309469121, 'DNA methylation signatures of early-life adversity are exposure-dependent in wild baboons')

nodes.label: Inbreeding avoidance mechanisms
nodes.description: How group-living primates avoid mating with close genetic relatives despite proximity — in wild chimpanzees, genetic relatedness estimates from exome-capture sequencing show females actively avoid close kin as mates even where both sexes sometimes remain in their natal community (bisexual philopatry), including detection of a rare, cryptic inbreeding event.

provenance.source: curator-drafted; grounded in White, Städele, Ramirez Amaya, Langergraber & Vigilant (2024, Royal Society Open Science 11(1):230967, doi:10.1098/rsos.230967, 'Female chimpanzees avoid inbreeding even in the presence of substantial bisexual philopatry')

nodes.label: Attachment styles in wild primates
nodes.description: The first systematic test of human-derived attachment-style classification (organized/secure vs. insecure, disorganized) in a wild great ape — 50 Taï chimpanzee offspring aged 0-10, followed for nearly 3,800 observation hours, showed organized attachment patterns resembling human infants but no behavioral evidence of disorganized attachment, informing comparative theory on the evolutionary origins of human-specific caregiving vulnerabilities.

provenance.source: curator-drafted; grounded in Rolland, Nodé-Langlois, Tkaczynski, Girard-Buttoz, Rayson, Crockford & Wittig (2025, Nature Human Behaviour 9:1571-1582, doi:10.1038/s41562-025-02176-8, 'Evidence of organized but not disorganized attachment in wild Western chimpanzee offspring')

nodes.label: Adult social play as cooperation scaffolding
nodes.description: Among adult (not just juvenile) wild chimpanzees, social play preceding a collective action — cooperative hunting, border patrols — increased the subsequent success of that cooperation, suggesting play functions to calibrate coordination and trust among adult cooperative partners, not just as a developmental practice arena for the young.

provenance.source: curator-drafted; grounded in Samuni, Mielke, Crockford & Wittig (2024, Current Biology, doi:10.1016/j.cub.2024.10.058, 'Social play fosters cooperation in wild adult chimpanzees')

nodes.label: Pan-African chimpanzee cultural and behavioral diversity
nodes.description: Comparing 144 behaviors across 46 chimpanzee communities found substantially more cultural diversity than any single-site study could reveal, and that environmental variability itself — not just genetic distance between populations — predicts how behaviorally diverse a community's repertoire is, complicating any simple story of culture spreading outward from one origin point.

provenance.source: curator-drafted; grounded in Kalan, Kulik, Arandjelovic, Boesch, Haas, Dieguez et al. & Kühl (2020, Nature Communications, doi:10.1038/s41467-020-18176-3, 'Environmental variability supports chimpanzee behavioural diversity') and Boesch, Kalan, Mundry, Arandjelovic, Pika, Dieguez et al. & Kühl (2020, Nature Human Behaviour, doi:10.1038/s41562-020-0890-1, 'Chimpanzee ethnography reveals unexpected cultural diversity'); both DOIs Crossref-verified 2026-09-04

nodes.label: Accumulative stone throwing and tree-directed behavior
nodes.description: A previously undocumented, ritualized-looking chimpanzee behavior — repeatedly throwing or banging stones against the same trees, building up piles of stones and creating characteristic bark damage — recorded via camera trap at multiple West African sites, resembling human cairn-building enough to raise open questions about whether it reflects a form of symbolic or ritual-like behavior, though the function remains genuinely unresolved rather than settled.

provenance.source: curator-drafted; grounded in Kühl, Kalan, Arandjelovic, Aubert, D'Auvergne, Goedmakers et al. & Boesch (2016, Scientific Reports, doi:10.1038/srep22219, 'Chimpanzee accumulative stone throwing'); DOI Crossref-verified 2026-09-04

nodes.label: Primate archaeology and accidental tool manufacture
