nodes.description: Applying archaeological excavation and lithic-analysis methods directly to living, observable primate tool-use sites, rather than only to the fossil/lithic record — wild bearded capuchin monkeys in Brazil, striking stones to lick mineral residue, unintentionally produce sharp stone flakes indistinguishable from classic early-hominin (Oldowan-type) tools, with no evidence the capuchins use the flakes for cutting; wild long-tailed macaques in Thailand develop distinct, group-specific tool-use 'archaeological signatures' even where ecology is shared, showing environment alone cannot explain the pattern.

provenance.source: curator-drafted; grounded in Proffitt, Luncz, Falótico, Ottoni, de la Torre & Haslam (2016, Nature, doi:10.1038/nature20112, 'Wild monkeys flake stone tools') and Luncz, Gill, Proffitt, Svensson, Kulik & Malaivijitnond (2019, eLife, doi:10.7554/eLife.46961, 'Group-specific archaeological signatures of stone tool use in wild macaques') — both DOIs verified live via literaturebase_verify_doi

nodes.label: Long-term field sites in primate range countries
nodes.description: PrimEvo's core method — decades-long individual-based field observation — depends on sustained local partnership: field assistants, trackers, and community relationships that make the data possible, and that are easy to erase from how the resulting science gets told.

provenance.source: curator-drafted; grounded in documented critiques of parachute/extractive field science and calls for equitable field-research partnership

nodes.label: Captive primate cognition and behavior research
nodes.description: The department's public identity is built on wild-population fieldwork, so any captive-facility component needs its own explicit, non-evasive framing rather than being folded silently into 'primate research' generally.

provenance.source: curator-drafted; grounded in documented zoo-based primate research practice at MPI-EVA-affiliated facilities

nodes.label: Genetic sampling and hormone/health monitoring of wild populations
nodes.description: The department's methods are designed around minimizing disturbance to wild populations, but a lay reader encountering 'genetic sampling' or 'hormone monitoring' without that context may assume capture, sedation, or other invasive procedures.

provenance.source: curator-drafted; grounded in standard non-invasive sampling practice in behavioral ecology and primatology

nodes.label: Developmental psychology
nodes.description: The study of how cognition, social understanding, and behavior change across childhood, providing the age-graded framework CCP tests cross-culturally.

nodes.label: Cultural psychology
nodes.description: The theory that mind and culture mutually constitute each other, motivating comparison of psychological processes across societies rather than assuming universality.

nodes.label: Social cognition
nodes.description: The study of mental processes underlying how individuals perceive, interpret, and respond to social information about others.

nodes.label: Theory of mind
nodes.description: The capacity to attribute mental states — beliefs, desires, intentions — to oneself and others, and to understand that these can differ from one's own or from reality. Central subject of the metarepresentation knowledge graph now hosted in ccp_module.

nodes.label: Learning biases
nodes.description: Systematic predispositions in how children selectively attend to and learn from social information, e.g. preferring prestigious, familiar, or majority models.

nodes.label: Individual-differences approach to cross-cultural cognition
nodes.description: A stated methodological pivot in CCP's own current research program: supplementing group-level cross-cultural comparison (society A vs. society B) with individual-level analysis, to identify which specific cultural and ecological factors actually drive cognitive-developmental variation, rather than treating 'culture' as a single undifferentiated between-group variable.

provenance.source: curator-drafted; grounded in Bohn, Fong, Pope-Caldwell, Stengelin & Haun (2024, Nature Reviews Psychology 3(10):641-643, doi:10.1038/s44159-024-00351-8, 'Understanding cultural variation in cognition one child at a time')

nodes.label: Children
nodes.description: Child participants across age ranges, the core study population for tracing the developmental emergence of social-cognitive capacities.

nodes.label: Cross-cultural samples
nodes.description: Study populations drawn from multiple societies, used to test whether developmental patterns found in one culture (often WEIRD samples) generalize.

nodes.label: Parenting
nodes.description: Caregiving practices and their cross-cultural variation, studied as a key input shaping children's social and cognitive development.

nodes.label: Social norms
nodes.description: Shared behavioral expectations within a community, studied for how and when children come to understand and enforce them.

nodes.label: Moral development
nodes.description: The emergence of moral judgment, fairness concerns, and prosocial behavior across childhood and across cultures.

nodes.label: Communication
nodes.description: The development of communicative and language abilities, studied as both a cognitive capacity and a social tool for coordinating with others.

nodes.label: Global Child Study Network
nodes.description: CCP's federated network of child-testing field stations spanning Congo, Cameroon, Malaysia, Namibia, Rossel Island (Papua New Guinea), and Uganda, complementing the Leipzig-based Child Study Centre — a far broader cross-cultural footprint than the single historical Namibia site this graph previously represented CCP's fieldwork with.

provenance.source: curator-drafted; grounded in CCP's own stated field infrastructure, eva.mpg.de/comparative-cultural-psychology/

nodes.label: Great ape comparative sample
nodes.description: Captive chimpanzees, bonobos, gorillas, and orangutans tested alongside human children on matched cognitive tasks — the comparative side of CCP's cross-species work, run through the Wolfgang Köhler Primate Research Center and led by Christoph Völter's Pan Cultures group, which studies which 'building blocks' of culture are shared across the four great-ape genera versus elaborated uniquely in humans.

provenance.source: curator-drafted; grounded in Christoph Völter's Pan Cultures group (current CCP research group, eva.mpg.de/comparative-cultural-psychology/) and Kaminski, Stengelin, Girndt, Haun & Liebal (2024, PLOS ONE 19(1):e0295221, doi:10.1371/journal.pone.0295221)

nodes.label: Behavioral experiments
nodes.description: Controlled tasks presented to children (or comparative non-human samples) that isolate specific cognitive or social capacities.

nodes.label: Eye-tracking
nodes.description: Recording gaze patterns to infer attention, expectation, and understanding in infants and children who cannot yet give verbal responses.

nodes.label: Cross-cultural surveys
nodes.description: Structured questionnaires administered across societies to compare beliefs, values, and reported practices.

nodes.label: Developmental tasks
nodes.description: Age-calibrated experimental paradigms (e.g. false-belief tasks) designed to detect the emergence of specific cognitive milestones.

nodes.label: Computational modeling
nodes.description: Formal and simulation-based models of cognitive or social-learning processes, used to generate testable predictions about developmental trajectories.

nodes.label: Cooperation development
nodes.description: How the capacity and motivation for cooperative behavior emerges and changes across childhood, and how this trajectory varies across cultures.

nodes.label: Fairness
nodes.description: The developmental and cross-cultural emergence of fairness concerns and equitable resource distribution.

nodes.label: Norm acquisition
nodes.description: How children come to recognize, internalize, and enforce the social norms of their community.

nodes.label: Cultural variation in cognition
nodes.description: The extent to which cognitive processes long assumed universal actually vary systematically across cultural contexts.

nodes.label: Communication development
nodes.description: How communicative and language capacities emerge and how their developmental trajectory relates to social cognition more broadly.

nodes.label: Cross-cultural norm enforcement in children
nodes.description: Whether children's willingness to intervene when a peer breaks a rule is a human universal or a culturally specific behavior — testing 5-8-year-olds across 8 diverse small-scale and large-scale societies found children everywhere enforced a novel game's conventional rules, but the style of enforcement (imperative protest vs. rule-citing protest) varied culturally, showing the underlying motivation is universal while its expression is not.

provenance.source: curator-drafted; grounded in Kanngiesser, Schäfer, Herrmann, Zeidler, Haun & Tomasello (2022, PNAS 119(2):e2112521118, doi:10.1073/pnas.2112521118, 'Children across societies enforce conventional norms but in culturally variable ways')

nodes.label: Inferring others' preferences across species and cultures
nodes.description: Whether anticipating a competitor's choice from their known preferences is a distinctly human, cross-culturally recurrent capacity — children from three culturally diverse societies (Namibia, Germany, Samoa) showed this ability consistently, while four tested great-ape species (chimpanzee, bonobo, gorilla, orangutan) did not, in a direct comparative design run alongside the department's Pan Cultures work.

provenance.source: curator-drafted; grounded in Kaminski, Stengelin, Girndt, Haun & Liebal (2024, PLOS ONE 19(1):e0295221, doi:10.1371/journal.pone.0295221, 'Understanding others' preferences: A comparison across primate species and human societies')

nodes.label: Individual differences in great ape cognition
nodes.description: Testing captive great apes across five cognitive tasks found individual performance was stable and repeatable over time, and predicted by each ape's own developmental rearing conditions — establishing that within-species individual variation, not just between-species differences, structures great ape cognition, drawing on the same WKPRC infrastructure behind this dataset's EVApeCognition fieldsite.

provenance.source: curator-drafted; grounded in Bohn, Eckert, Hanus, Lugauer, Holtmann & Haun (2023, Nature Ecology & Evolution 7:927-938, doi:10.1038/s41559-023-02050-8, 'Great ape cognition is structured by stable cognitive abilities and predicted by developmental conditions')

nodes.label: Zoo-based great ape cognition research
nodes.description: CCP's comparative-cognition work with chimpanzees, bonobos, orangutans, and gorillas is largely conducted at zoo-based research centers rather than in the wild, which is scientifically valuable (controlled comparison, longitudinal access) but publicly legible mainly through the lens of 'apes in captivity.'

provenance.source: curator-drafted; grounded in documented zoo-based great-ape cognition research practice at MPI-EVA-affiliated facilities

nodes.label: Cross-cultural research with children
nodes.description: CCP's comparative developmental work depends on running the same or comparable tasks with children from societies with very different childrearing practices, economies, and relationships to outside researchers — a design that only works, and only remains ethical, with genuine informed consent and ongoing trust from families and communities.

provenance.source: curator-drafted; grounded in documented critiques of WEIRD-sample bias in developmental psychology (Henrich, Heine & Norenzayan 2010) and cross-cultural research-ethics practice

nodes.label: Anthropomorphism vs. anthropodenial in reporting animal cognition
nodes.description: CCP's core scientific contribution is often exactly the nuanced middle ground — what a species does and doesn't share with human cognition — but that nuance is the first thing lost in translation to a headline or exhibit caption.

provenance.source: curator-drafted; grounded in the anthropomorphism/anthropodenial framing from comparative cognition science communication literature (de Waal 1999)

nodes.label: Selection and Adaptation — Genetic and Biological
nodes.description: Selection and adaptation are, at the most general level, substrate-neutral: 'selection' is any process by which a feature increases in frequency because of its consequences in an environment, and 'adaptation' is any feature that evolved in a population because it contributed to fitness. This node covers the specific case where the feature under selection is heritable and genetically encoded — the instantiation four MPI-EVA departments study directly: DAG and EvoGen detect it as a genomic signature (selective sweeps, reduced diversity around a locus), HumOr reconstructs it from skeletal/dental adaptation in the fossil record, and PrimEvo studies its sexual-selection variant shaping primate mating systems. It has a companion node, inst-theory-cultural-and-behavioral-selection-and-adaptation, for the non-genetic case — behavioral, cognitive, and cultural variants selected and retained without a genetic mechanism doing the selecting — which is the primary purview of DLCE, HBEC, and CCP rather than a peripheral concern of this node's four departments.

provenance.source: derived from mpi-eva-graph/sub-units department node overlap

nodes.label: Selection and Adaptation — Cultural and Behavioral
nodes.description: The companion case to inst-theory-selection-and-adaptation: the same general mechanism — a feature persisting or spreading because of its consequences in an environment — applied to behavioral, cognitive, and cultural variants rather than genes. HBEC's and DLCE's cultural-evolution theories treat cultural traits (skills, beliefs, practices, and — for DLCE specifically — linguistic and narrative forms) as undergoing variation, selection, and inheritance analogous to, but mechanistically distinct from, biological evolution; CCP's learning-biases theory names the selective-retention mechanism itself — which models and information children preferentially copy, i.e. which variants actually get selected during transmission. None of this requires a genetic substrate: DLCE and CCP do not study genes at all, and for HBEC genetics is one contributing strand among several rather than the department's organizing framework — unlike the four departments behind this node's companion.

provenance.source: derived from mpi-eva-graph/sub-units department node overlap, added in response to direct critique of the original node's framing

nodes.label: Cultural Transmission and Social Learning
nodes.description: The theory that behaviors, skills, and beliefs spread through populations by observation, imitation, and teaching rather than genetic inheritance alone — HBEC's and DLCE's own cultural-evolution and social-learning theories treat this directly, CCP studies the learning biases that shape which models and information children preferentially copy, and PrimEvo documents its behavioral signature as socially learned tool-use traditions in wild primates.

provenance.source: derived from mpi-eva-graph/sub-units department node overlap

nodes.label: Life History Theory
nodes.description: The evolutionary framework explaining how organisms allocate finite resources between growth, reproduction, and survival across the lifespan — applied by HBEC and PrimEvo to living human and primate populations respectively, and by HumOr to the fossil and dental evidence of how that allocation pattern itself evolved across hominin lineages.

provenance.source: derived from mpi-eva-graph/sub-units department node overlap

nodes.label: Population Structure and Demography
nodes.description: How population size, structure, and vital rates are organized and change over time. DAG and EvoGen reconstruct this from genomic variation (paleodemography, effective population size, demographic bottlenecks), HBEC studies it directly through fieldwork in living small-scale societies, and PrimEvo tracks group size, sex ratio, and age structure in wild primate populations.

provenance.source: derived from mpi-eva-graph/sub-units department node overlap

nodes.label: Migration and Dispersal
nodes.description: The movement of individuals and populations across landscapes, and its downstream social and genetic consequences. DAG reconstructs ancient human migration waves from genomic transects, HumOr traces hominin dispersal from fossil and archaeological distributions, HBEC studies residential and logistical mobility patterns in living societies, and PrimEvo studies natal dispersal's effect on primate gene flow, social structure, and inbreeding avoidance.

provenance.source: derived from mpi-eva-graph/sub-units department node overlap

nodes.label: Ancient and Archaic Genomes
nodes.description: Genomic material recovered from ancient or archaic (non-modern) hominin remains — DAG's core ancient-DNA domain and the degraded, contaminated samples it specializes in extracting and authenticating, EvoGen's archaic-hominin-genomes domain used for downstream population-genetic analysis, and HumOr's paleogenomics domain that integrates that same evidence with fossil and archaeological context.

provenance.source: derived from mpi-eva-graph/sub-units department node overlap

nodes.label: Phylogenetic and Tree-Based Inference Methods
nodes.description: Statistical methods that model lineages as branching trees to reconstruct relationships and divergence times. DAG and EvoGen apply this to genomic and population lineages (phylogenetics, phylogenomic analysis), DLCE applies the same Bayesian tree-inference machinery to language and cultural-trait lineages instead of genes, and HBEC applies phylogenetic comparative methods to correct for shared ancestry when statistically comparing populations or species.

provenance.source: derived from mpi-eva-graph/sub-units department node overlap

nodes.label: Cooperation and Fairness
nodes.description: Open questions about why individuals cooperate and how norms of fair exchange emerge and are enforced. HBEC's largest single topic cluster (cooperation, fairness, punishment, partner choice) studies this in living human societies; PrimEvo studies its coalition- and alliance-formation precursors in wild primates; CCP studies when and how children acquire cooperative behavior and fairness concerns developmentally and cross-culturally.

provenance.source: derived from mpi-eva-graph/sub-units department node overlap

nodes.label: Archaic Introgression
nodes.description: The open question of how much, when, and with what functional consequences anatomically modern humans interbred with archaic hominins such as Neanderthals and Denisovans. DAG studies it through admixture modeling and Neanderthal-admixture case work, EvoGen through genomic analysis of the functional and phenotypic consequences of introgressed variants persisting today, and HumOr through the fossil and genomic biology of the archaic populations themselves.

provenance.source: derived from mpi-eva-graph/sub-units department node overlap

nodes.label: Animal research and public perception
nodes.description: CCP's comparative cognition work is largely zoo-based (Leipzig Zoo's Wolfgang Köhler Primate Research Center); PrimEvo combines wild-population field observation with some captive-facility and non-invasive sampling work; EvoGen functionally validates human-evolutionary genetic variants in mouse models. All three require the same basic communication discipline: name the animal, the facility or field context, the welfare oversight, and the specific method, rather than either hiding the animal-research component or over-dramatizing it.

provenance.source: derived from mpi-eva-graph/sub-units department scicomm_sensitivities.json overlap

nodes.label: Human remains, fossils, and repatriation
nodes.description: DAG's version centers on ancient-DNA sampling of skeletal remains and the field-wide 2021 guidance on responsible ancient-human-remains research; HumOr's centers on fossil collections with colonial-era acquisition histories and the need for genuine host-country research partnership. Different material (genetic material vs. fossil specimens), same underlying obligation: name the consultation, consent, or partnership process whenever findings from remains are communicated publicly.

provenance.source: derived from mpi-eva-graph/sub-units department scicomm_sensitivities.json overlap

nodes.label: Oversimplified evolutionary and genetic narratives
nodes.description: DAG and EvoGen both generate the 'percent Neanderthal' oversimplification from different methods (demographic admixture modeling vs. functional genomics); EvoGen's disease-variant findings and DAG's population-structure findings both risk genetic-determinist and racialized misreadings; HumOr's fossil record is popularly flattened into linear 'March of Progress' narratives that misrepresent its actual branching structure. All three call for the same discipline: lead public communication with the specific mechanism and its demographic or evolutionary explanation, not an aggregate statistic or a single-line narrative.

provenance.source: derived from mpi-eva-graph/sub-units department scicomm_sensitivities.json overlap

nodes.label: Community consent and benefit-sharing in research with living communities
nodes.description: HBEC's hunter-gatherer and small-scale-society fieldwork, DLCE's endangered-language documentation, CCP's cross-cultural child research, PrimEvo's field sites in primate range countries, and EvoGen's diverse genomic sample panels are methodologically very different, but each depends on a research relationship with a specific community that has, across the wider field's history, sometimes been extractive rather than reciprocal. The most natural institute-wide sensitivity in this dataset — it is the only scicomm theme that reaches a genuine majority of departments (5 of 7) rather than a tight 2–3-department cluster.

provenance.source: derived from mpi-eva-graph/sub-units department scicomm_sensitivities.json overlap

nodes.label: Denisova Cave
nodes.description: The single cave where a 2010 finger-bone DNA analysis revealed the Denisovans, a previously unknown archaic hominin lineage — the founding discovery of MPI-EVA's paleogenomics program and still an active dual-department excavation/sequencing site.

nodes.label: Vindija Cave
nodes.description: Source cave of the high-coverage Neandertal genome (sequenced from a bone found in 1980) that let MPI-EVA researchers identify additional Neandertal ancestry in present-day non-African populations.

nodes.label: Issyk Kurgan
nodes.description: One of ~45 royal kurgans at this Iron Age Saka burial ground, excavated since 1969 and famous for the 'Golden Man' warrior burial (c. 400–300 BCE) — the site of the first genome-wide ancient-DNA data from that individual, generated as part of a 2026 DAG study finding political power passed through elite family lineages across Eurasian steppe burial sites.

nodes.label: Jebel Irhoud
nodes.description: Site of fossils redated in 2017 to ~300,000 years ago — by far the oldest securely dated Homo sapiens remains known, pushing the species' origin back roughly 100,000 years and reframing it as a pan-African rather than single-region event.

nodes.label: Thomas Quarry I
nodes.description: Cave-complex quarry site on Casablanca's Atlantic littoral, part of an internationally important Plio-Pleistocene coastal archive — a 2026 study redated hominin fossils here (alongside sister site Oulad Hamida) to ~773,000 years, among the oldest well-dated hominin remains in North Africa.

nodes.label: Taï National Park
nodes.description: MPI-EVA's flagship wild-chimpanzee field site, continuously studied since 1979 — the source of foundational findings on wild chimpanzee tool use and tool making, still an active multi-camp research station, today organizationally part of HBEC (Crockford & Wittig) though its findings remain PrimEvo's natural conceptual domain.

provenance.source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Taï_National_Park, latlong.net Taï National Park entry, eva.mpg.de/fileadmin/content_files/staff/boesch/pdf/pan_af_new_tai_chimp_proj.pdf, karger.com Folia Primatologica 54(1-2)

nodes.label: Amboseli National Park
nodes.description: Site of the Amboseli Baboon Research Project, a continuous, individual-based study of wild yellow/anubis-hybrid baboons founded by Stuart and Jeanne Altmann in 1971 — life-history data on 1,500+ known individuals across five decades, still monitoring roughly 300 animals near-daily today.

nodes.label: Pemba Island
nodes.description: Long-running (since 2015) HBEC field site studying community-based resource-management institutions, household economic adaptation, and tropical coastal-ecosystem conservation, including REDD+ forest-carbon program evaluation.

provenance.source: eva.mpg.de/ecology/fieldwork/pemba.html, cambridge.org Oryx article page, en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pemba_Island

nodes.label: Motaba River (BaYaka research camp)
nodes.description: A Motaba River BaYaka/Bandongo research area studied by two MPI-EVA departments: HBEC's own work on collaborative foraging and childcare/subsistence trade-offs (this node's primary research_output), and CCP's separate study of children's sharing-norm development — HBEC's second real field site alongside Pemba, added specifically as the example this repo's fieldsites/README.md had already flagged as its next natural addition; the CCP connection surfaced afterward while checking whether CCP had its own genuine Congo Basin presence.

provenance.source: pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC9667358/ (fetched directly), doi.org/10.1098/rspb.2022.1407, doi.org/10.1371/journal.pone.0276845, en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dongou, en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Motaba

nodes.label: Emae Island
nodes.description: One of four small-scale multilingualism case-study sites (alongside North Malekula and Maewo Island) documented by MPI-EVA's Comparative Oceanic Linguistics group across Vanuatu's 65 inhabited islands, each with its own distinct linguistic ecology.

nodes.label: Maewo Island
nodes.description: One of the study's four small-scale multilingualism case-study sites — Maewo (Penama Province, ~1,400 speakers of Sungwadaga/Central Maewo per Ethnologue-derived sources) is linguistically and ecologically distinct from Emae's Shepherd Islands setting, part of what makes the four-site comparison meaningful.

nodes.label: North Malekula
nodes.description: One of the study's four small-scale multilingualism case-study sites — north Malekula is one of the most linguistically dense areas in Vanuatu (itself one of the world's most linguistically dense countries), with numerous small, distinct language communities packed into a small geographic area.

nodes.label: Wolfgang Köhler Primate Research Center
nodes.description: MPI-EVA's captive great-ape cognition testing facility at Leipzig Zoo, source of EVApeCognition — an 18-year (2004–2021), 246-study, 105-named-participant open dataset spanning chimpanzees, bonobos, gorillas, and orangutans, described on its 2026 publication as the largest open dataset of great ape cognition in existence. This repo's own assets/CCP/evape-cognition-oecs/ mirrors a curated slice of it, and js/evape-db-explorer.js is a live whiteboard artifact built directly on that data.

provenance.source: mpg.de/26395591/largest-open-dataset-of-great-ape-cognition-released, eurekalert.org/news-releases/1125110, eva.mpg.de/comparative-cultural-psychology/studying-non-human-primates/wolfgang-koehler-primate-research-center/, this repo's own assets/CCP/evape-cognition-oecs/manifest.json and processed/evapecognition-db-explorer.json

nodes.label: Ilsenhöhle, Ranis
nodes.description: A rock shelter beneath Ranis Castle where ~45,000-year-old modern human remains were recovered and sequenced, constraining the timing of the single major Neanderthal admixture pulse into non-African populations to roughly 45,000-49,000 years ago, over a window estimated at about 7,000 years. A companion 2024 paper (McPherron, Hublin et al.) separately attributed the site's LRJ stone-tool assemblage to these same H. sapiens, one of the earliest secure H. sapiens presences at high European latitudes.

provenance.source: nature.com/articles/s41586-024-08420-x; nature.com/articles/s41586-023-06923-7; general-knowledge placement of Ranis, Thuringia — not independently verified against site-specific geodata in this pass

nodes.label: Swartkrans
nodes.description: A cave site in South Africa's Cradle of Humankind where a rare, directly associated hip bone, femur, and tibia of a small adult Paranthropus robustus (c. 1.7 million years old) were described in 2025 — new direct evidence for this species' posture and gait, distinct from the locomotor pattern already documented for Australopithecus at nearby Sterkfontein.

provenance.source: doi.org/10.1016/j.jhevol.2024.103647; general-knowledge placement of Swartkrans — not independently verified against site-specific geodata in this pass

nodes.label: Kara-Djigach cemetery
nodes.description: One of two 1338-1339 CE Chüy Valley cemeteries (with sister site Burana) where ancient DNA from plague victims identified a Yersinia pestis strain genetically ancestral to the Black Death's explosive 14th-century diversification — pinpointing Central Asia, not the Black Sea/Crimea, as the pandemic's geographic source. Directly grounds Johannes Krause's 2026 Leibniz Prize citation for 'an evidence-based understanding of the history of epidemics.'

provenance.source: nature.com/articles/s41586-022-04800-3; general-knowledge placement of the Chüy Valley — not independently verified against site-specific geodata in this pass

nodes.label: Inuvialuit Settlement Region
nodes.description: A real, current HBEC field site (the Sanguatsiniq Research Project) studying Inuit subsistence harvesting, foraging, and carbon economics in Canada's western Arctic — Bayesian estimation shows local harvesting is substantially more carbon-efficient than market-food substitutes, direct evidence for how Indigenous subsistence economies interact with encroaching market and carbon economies.

provenance.source: doi.org/10.1073/pnas.2317686121; eva.mpg.de/ecology/projects-and-research-groups/; general-knowledge placement of the Inuvialuit Settlement Region — not independently verified against site-specific geodata in this pass

nodes.label: Rising Star Cave System (Dinaledi Chamber)
nodes.description: A deep, extremely hard-to-access chamber (the Dinaledi Chamber) within the Rising Star Cave System where over 1,550 fossil elements of Homo naledi — a small-brained, mosaic-anatomy hominin combining primitive and derived traits, including notably dexterous hands — were recovered starting in 2013, named and described in 2015.

provenance.source: elifesciences.org/articles/09560 (DOI Crossref-verified 2026-09-04); general-knowledge placement of the Rising Star Cave System — not independently verified against site-specific geodata in this pass

nodes.label: Bili-Uélé Forest
nodes.description: A vast (~50,000 km² surveyed, within a ~78,000 km² protected-area complex), remote forest region in northern DRC where a large, continuous population of several thousand Eastern chimpanzees (Pan troglodytes schweinfurthii) was documented — a PanAf field site distinctive for a rich, unusual toolkit (large termite-fishing tools, nut-cracking, possible ant-dipping wands) and the accumulative stone-throwing behavior first recorded here alongside other West/Central African sites.

nodes.label: Oshikoto Region (Akhoe Haiǁom communities)
nodes.description: Field site for cross-cultural cognitive-science research with the Akhoe Haiǁom, a semi-nomadic hunter-gatherer community in northern Namibia whose language encodes spatial relations very differently from German/English — the basis for an early, influential MPI-EVA line of research on how culture and language shape memory and spatial cognition.

provenance.source: eva.mpg.de/documents/Elsevier/Haun_Variation_CurrBiol_2009_1554168.pdf (fetched and read directly 2026-09-04, acknowledgments section), open-web search placing Khomxa Khoeda Junior Primary School and Farm Six in Mangetti West near Tsumeb, en.wikipedia.org/wiki/ǂAakhoe_dialect, sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S0960982209018983, eva.mpg.de/comparative-cultural-psychology/staff/daniel-haun/
